{{nihongo|'''Hajikami Shrine'''|㯮椒神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Tajima Province]].

'''Hajikami Shrine'''<ref group="注">The first character (㯮) is wood-radical + 蜀.</ref> (はじかみじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} in {{ill|Takeno, Hyōgo|Q7678035|qid=Q7678035}}, {{ill|Toyooka, Hyōgo|Q696388|qid=Q696388}}, {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|Q130290|qid=Q130290}}. It stands on a mountain summit in the Hajikami settlement, with the Sanchō River below. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|fr|Myōjin Taisha|ja|名神大社|simple|Myōjin Taisha|zh|名神大社|qid=Q9610964}}), and its former rank was {{ill|Son-sha|Q134917284|qid=Q134917284}}. Some sources read the shrine name as "Hosoki"<ref>Side-reading notes in manuscript copies of ''Engishiki'', and also ''Hyogo Prefecture Encyclopedia'' (1983), Kobe Shimbun Publishing Center.</ref>.

== Enshrined deity ==
* '''Hajikami Ōkami''' (はじかみのおおかみ)
** Because Hajikami settlement produced {{ill|Asakura sanshō|Q109598996|qid=Q109598996}}, there is a theory it was worshipped as a local land deity<ref name="Kyōbusho">''{{ill|Tokusen Jinmyōchō|Q11571092|qid=Q11571092}}''.</ref>; another theory sees it as deification of {{ill|Zanthoxylum schinifolium|Q15249901|qid=Q15249901}}<ref>''History of Toyooka City'' Vol.1, Toyooka City, 1981.</ref>, but details are unclear. One theory says it enshrines {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōyama-mori-no-Mikoto}}<ref name="Kokushi documents">"Keta District Old Tales" in ''{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kokushi Monjo}}''. ''Kokushi Monjo'' is said to have been compiled in 975 by a person named Yōkō Mashika and is often treated as doubtful, though some accept old traditions within it (Keiichi Imai, ''Ame no Hiboko'', Sōgeisha, 1966). See also {{ill|koshi koden|Q11410976|qid=Q11410976}}.</ref>, but its textual basis is questioned<ref name="prev note">See previous note.</ref>.

== Origin ==
The site has long connected to the {{ill|Toyooka Basin|Q11633476|qid=Q11633476}} by routes crossing Banya Pass to the east or Ōta-goe to the south via {{ill|Kannabe Highlands|Q11591007|qid=Q11591007}}, and via river transport on the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Nasa River}} and {{ill|Inanba River|Q16277514|qid=Q16277514}} to the provincial center of {{ill|Tajima Province|Q1053727|qid=Q1053727}}; links with the kokufu are assumed<ref name="report">''Shikinaisha Survey Report''.</ref>. It has also been pointed out that this shrine may relate to the one to (斗) of "Hajikami" medicine herb that Tajima had to present under the "miscellaneous medicines from provinces" section in the {{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}}<ref name="Kyōbusho"/>.

According to shrine tradition, in {{ill|Hakuhō|Q11580612|qid=Q11580612}} 14 ({{ill|685|Q33480|qid=Q33480}}), the Tajima provincial governor Haibara no Kimi Kagamaro enshrined his ancestor Ōyama-mori-no-Mikoto, and in the next year ({{ill|Shuchō|Q777413|qid=Q777413}} 1 / {{ill|686|Q30619|qid=Q30619}}) oil pressed from local sanshō fruit was presented to the imperial court<ref name="Kokushi documents"/>; however, reliability is questioned<ref name="prev note"/>. In {{ill|Jōwa (Heian period)|Q1075605|qid=Q1075605|lt=Jōwa}} 9 ({{ill|842|Q24730|qid=Q24730}}), it entered the official shrine register<ref>''{{ill|Shoku Nihon Kōki|Q1041301|qid=Q1041301}}'', entry for 15th day, 10th month, same year.</ref>, and in {{ill|Jōgan|Q1075635|qid=Q1075635|lt=Jōgan}} 10 ({{ill|869|Q23917|qid=Q23917}}) it was promoted from Junior Fifth Rank Lower to Junior Fifth Rank Upper<ref>''{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981}}'', entry for 27th day, 12th month, same year.</ref>. Under the Engi system it was listed as a myojin taisha. Notably, other Tajima myojin taisha ({{ill|Yama Shrine|Q21655261|qid=Q21655261|lt=Yama}}, {{ill|Tono Shrine|Q21655262|qid=Q21655262|lt=To}}, {{ill|Raijin Shrine (Toyooka)|Q21655264|qid=Q21655264|lt=Ikazuchi}}, and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Watatsumi}}) likewise entered the official register and rose to Junior Fifth Rank Upper at the same time.

At an unknown date, Hachiman deity appears to have been invited from {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Q710098|qid=Q710098}} in {{ill|Yamashiro Province|Q749276|qid=Q749276}}. From the medieval period onward, as "Masu (Hajikami) Betsugū," it was counted as one of the Tajima eight branch shrines of Iwashimizu<ref>e.g., imperial proclamation dated Dec 3, {{ill|Hōgen (era)|Q1193898|qid=Q1193898}} 3 (1158), in {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū documents}}.</ref>. In the Tajima provincial {{ill|Ōtabumi|Q1413174|qid=Q1413174}} dated {{ill|Kōan (Kamakura period)|Q389180|qid=Q389180}} 8 ({{ill|1285|Q5546|qid=Q5546}}), it appears as "Hachiman-gū territory, Hajikami Betsugū," showing it was the guardian shrine of an Iwashimizu estate and was henceforth mainly called "Hachimangū." It also had deep ties with {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōoka-ji (Toyooka)}} on Mt. Ōoka's slope; records state this shrine's torii marked the northern boundary of that temple precinct<ref>Draft report on temple land and forests of Ōoka-ji, dated Aug 7, {{ill|Eiryaku|Q1193895|qid=Q1193895}} 2 (1161) ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōoka-ji documents}}).</ref>. In early modern times, Ōoka-ji is confirmed as its {{ill|Bettō-ji|Q11396755|qid=Q11396755}}<ref>munafuda of {{ill|Kanbun (era)|Q1146228|qid=Q1146228}} 9 (1669), and ''Kakiagechō'' of Kyōhō 20 (1735), etc. (''Takeno Town History: Folklore/Cultural Properties/Documents'').</ref>. Records from {{ill|Enpō|Q1145735|qid=Q1145735}} 7 ({{ill|1679|Q7638|qid=Q7638}}) and {{ill|Kyōhō|Q1145048|qid=Q1145048}} 6 ({{ill|1721|Q6913|qid=Q6913}}) show it held 7 se of shrine land around the site<ref group="注">Local place names such as "Otō-dani," "Miya-no-shita," "Dō-dani," and "Asō" are said to be remnants of shrine lands (''Takeno Town History: Folklore/Cultural Properties/Documents'').</ref>. Though mountainous, nearby gold mining by Ikuno magistrate formed a small mining settlement, and in {{ill|Tenpō|Q1369045|qid=Q1369045}} 5 ({{ill|1834|Q7591|qid=Q7591}}) the shrine had 140 parishioner households<ref name="report"/>.

In {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} 6 ({{ill|1873|Q7757|qid=Q7757}}) it was ranked village shrine; in Meiji 22 ({{ill|1889|Q7831|qid=Q7831}}) the honden was rebuilt and a heiden newly built; in {{ill|Shōwa era|Q327567|qid=Q327567}} 27 ({{ill|1952|Q5272|qid=Q5272}}) renovations were made around the honden.

== Rituals ==
Until the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Taishō period}}, festival day was old lunar Aug 15; later it changed to Sept 15 (solar), then Oct 1, and now Oct 15. Formerly, parishioners selected ritual officials called "kagiban," and rites were likely conducted through {{ill|miyaza|Q11454763|qid=Q11454763}} / {{ill|touya|Q11664931|qid=Q11664931}}<ref name="report"/><ref name="town history">''Takeno Town History: Folklore/Cultural Properties/Documents''.</ref>.

== Shrine buildings ==
The honden is a copper-roofed {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|Q3193781|qid=Q3193781}} rebuilt in Meiji 22. Other buildings include a tile-roofed gabled {{ill|Heiden (Shinto)|Q3076699|qid=Q3076699}}, an {{ill|East Asian hip-and-gable roof|Q855025|qid=Q855025}} {{ill|Haiden (Shinto)|Q3125745|qid=Q3125745}} with kokera roofing, and a board-roofed basket hall<ref name="report"/>.

== Sub-shrine ==
* Gion Shrine - at the north foot below the main shrine; enshrines a {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|Q854773|qid=Q854773}} image as honji-butsu. The Omaki-zakura stands before it.
It is said there was formerly also a Hachibashira Kōjin shrine<ref name="town history"/>.

== Cultural properties ==
; Designated by Toyooka City
:; Komainu
:: Wooden {{ill|Komainu|Q20155846|qid=Q20155846}} thought to be Muromachi period works. The {{ill|Agyō|Q137190281|qid=Q137190281}} is 69 cm high; the {{ill|Ungyō|Q137190286|qid=Q137190286}} is 60 cm. Both retain color, which is rare<ref>''Kadokawa Place Names Dictionary 28 Hyogo Prefecture'', Kadokawa Shoten, 1988.</ref>. Designated tangible cultural property of Takeno Town on Nov 15, 1977; after municipal merger became Toyooka city cultural property.
:; Omaki-zakura
{{Main|Omaki-zakura (Hyogo)}}
:: Edo-higan tree in front of the lower shrine (Gion Shrine), estimated age 500 years (as of 1991). Height 14.5 m, root girth 7 m, trunk girth at eye height 6.05 m; crown spread 15 m east-west and 18.5 m north-south, covering about 4 ares. Designated natural monument of Takeno Town on Mar 8, 1979; after merger became Toyooka city cultural property. Designated Hyogo Prefecture {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=local monument}} on Mar 29, 1996.
